vignette:
He is a 67-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life in courtrooms, speaking in a steady voice about facts, evidence, and the boundaries of the law. As a prosecutor, he is used to structuring painful stories into timelines that can be tolerated by a judge and jury. His own story does not arrange itself so neatly.

The assault happens more than three decades ago, when he is in his thirties and still early in his career. He has recently been assigned to a provincial office and is proud of the promotion, though he is also lonely, living away from family in a rented apartment. One evening after a work function, he accepts a ride from a man he knows professionally, someone older and well connected, someone he believes he cannot afford to offend. Instead of driving him home, the man takes him to another location. What follows is abrupt, coercive, and disorienting. He remembers the smell of alcohol, the pressure of a hand at the back of his neck, the humiliation of hearing his own voice become strange to him-first arguing, then pleading, then disappearing. What remains with him most sharply is not only fear, but disbelief: a stunned conviction that this cannot be happening to him, a man trained to read danger, a man whose work depends on authority.

In the days afterward, he goes to work as if nothing has happened. He tells no one. He avoids using the man's name and rearranges his schedule to reduce the chance of seeing him. When avoidance is impossible, he becomes stiff and overly formal, speaking in clipped legal phrases. He throws himself into work, staying late in the office and obsessively revising briefs. At night he sleeps lightly, waking in panic without immediately knowing why. Then the memory returns in fragments-a door closing, the weight of another body, the sickening sense of being trapped. He showers for a long time before work, scrubbing himself until his skin reddens, then feels ashamed by the ritual and even more ashamed that he cannot simply stop.

For years, he tells himself that silence is discipline. He marries, raises children, advances professionally. Outwardly he is respected, controlled, exacting. Inside, he lives with a private geometry of avoidance. He does not like closed offices with only one exit. He does not drink at professional gatherings. If a colleague stands too close behind him, his shoulders lock. He scans rooms automatically, choosing a seat with a clear view of the door. He becomes known as serious, even severe. His late wife sometimes asks why he startles so violently when she touches him unexpectedly in the kitchen, or why he goes quiet after certain scenes in films. He never finds words that feel survivable. He says only that work has made him tense.

In court, sexual assault cases affect him in ways he cannot explain. He remains composed, but afterward he is depleted and irritable, sometimes sitting alone in his car gripping the steering wheel until his hands ache. He is especially unsettled by witnesses who doubt themselves, by male victims who minimize what happened, by defense arguments that turn coercion into misunderstanding. He can hear the old commands he gave himself-don't make trouble, don't be weak, forget this. Some nights after these cases he dreams vividly and wakes drenched in sweat, his heart pounding as if he is back in that room. On those mornings he is curt with colleagues and then disgusted with himself.

His wife's death several years ago removes the person who, without knowing the details, helped anchor him. Since then, the symptoms feel less contained. Retirement has been discussed, but he resists it, partly because work gives structure to his days and partly because unoccupied time allows memories to rise. At home, the evenings are the hardest. He checks the locks repeatedly, though he knows this is irrational. He keeps the television on for noise but does not follow the plot. Certain colognes, leather upholstery, and the sound of a car door shutting nearby can pull him abruptly into a state of alarm. In those moments he feels both old and suddenly young, not in years but in helplessness.

What finally brings him to speak is not one dramatic collapse but cumulative exhaustion. A recent case involving an older male victim leaves him shaking in the restroom after court. He looks at himself in the mirror and is startled by how frightened he appears. In session, he speaks carefully at first, as though giving testimony. He corrects dates, clarifies context, apologizes when emotion interrupts the chronology. But as he returns to the memory, what emerges most powerfully is the enduring injury to his sense of self. He still thinks, at times, that he should have prevented it. He still feels contaminated by an act committed against him. He still lives as though danger is just behind him, close enough to touch.
